sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Overview of soil nail wall main elements, construction sequence, common highway applications, feasibility evaluation framework, and factors affecting costs. Provides the basis for engineers to make initial assessments of whether soil nailing is appropriate for a specific project.
sections.body: This chapter provides an overview of the main elements and the construction sequence of soil nail walls, along with common applications and project conditions favorable for the use of soil nailing. Feasibility evaluations and factors affecting costs are also discussed. The information in this chapter helps engineers make initial assessments of whether soil nailing is appropriate for a specific project.
key_points: Overview of main elements and construction sequence
Common applications for soil nailing in highway projects
Feasibility evaluation framework
Factors affecting project costs
sections.applicability: Initial project feasibility assessment for soil nail walls.

sections.title: Elements of a Soil Nail Wall
sections.summary: A soil nail wall has three main components: (1) soil nails—#6 to #10 threaded bars (19–32 mm), Grade 60/75, at 1.2–1.8 m spacing and 10–20° inclination, with centralizers and neat cement grout; (2) facing—initial 75–100 mm shotcrete with WWM and final 150–200 mm CIP or shotcrete; (3) ancillary elements including bearing plates, drainage strips, and toe drain.
sections.body: A soil nail wall system consists of three main components: (1) soil nails, including the steel tendon (solid or hollow bar), centralizers, grout (neat cement), and corrosion protection (epoxy coating or encapsulation); (2) the facing, which includes an initial facing (typically 75-100 mm shotcrete with WWM) and a final facing (150-200 mm CIP concrete or shotcrete); and (3) other components including bearing plates, hex nuts, washers, headed studs, geocomposite drainage strips, and a toe drain pipe. Soil nails are typically #6 to #10 (19 to 32 mm diameter) Grade 60 or Grade 75 threaded bars, installed at horizontal and vertical spacings of 1.2 to 1.8 m (4 to 6 ft) and inclinations of 10 to 20 degrees below horizontal.
key_points: Three main components: soil nails, facing, and ancillary elements
Soil nail tendons: #6 to #10 bars (19-32 mm), Grade 60 or 75
Typical spacing: 1.2-1.8 m horizontal and vertical
Typical inclination: 10-20 degrees below horizontal
Initial facing: 75-100 mm shotcrete with WWM
Final facing: 150-200 mm CIP concrete or shotcrete
Drainage: geocomposite strips and toe drain pipe

sections.title: Construction Sequence
sections.summary: Top-down construction proceeds in 1–2 m lifts: excavate, drill holes, install tendons with centralizers, grout from bottom up using tremie, install drainage strips, apply initial shotcrete facing with WWM, install bearing plates, then repeat for each lift. Final facing is installed after all nails are placed and initial facing is cured.
sections.body: Soil nail wall construction follows a top-down sequence: (1) excavate soil to a depth slightly below the next level of soil nails (typically 1-2 m lifts); (2) drill holes for soil nails at the design spacing and inclination; (3) install soil nail tendons with centralizers; (4) grout the drill holes using tremie method from bottom up; (5) install drainage strips if needed; (6) place initial facing of shotcrete with WWM over the exposed cut face; (7) install bearing plates and secure with hex nuts; (8) repeat steps 1-7 for subsequent lifts until full wall height is achieved; (9) install final facing after all nails are installed and initial facing is cured.
key_points: Top-down construction in 1-2 m lifts
Drill holes, install tendons with centralizers, grout from bottom up
Install drainage strips before shotcrete if needed
Apply initial shotcrete facing with WWM
Secure bearing plates with hex nuts
Repeat for each excavation lift
Install final facing after all nails are placed

sections.title: Applications of Soil Nail Walls
sections.summary: Common applications include roadway cut stabilization, bridge abutment excavation support, repair and reinforcement of existing retaining structures, tunnel portal stabilization, highway slope stabilization, and temporary excavation support. Most common wall heights are 4–12 m; maximum approximately 18 m.
sections.body: Common applications for soil nail walls include: (1) roadway cut stabilization for new alignments or widening; (2) excavation support for bridge abutments and end slopes; (3) stabilization of existing retaining structures by adding nails through the facing; (4) stabilization of tunnel portals; (5) slope stabilization adjacent to highways; (6) repair of existing retaining walls; and (7) temporary excavation support during construction. Soil nail walls have been successfully used for wall heights up to approximately 18 m (60 ft), although the most common range is 4 to 12 m (13 to 40 ft).
key_points: Roadway cuts for new alignments or widening
Excavation support for bridge abutments
Stabilization of existing retaining structures
Tunnel portal stabilization
Slope stabilization adjacent to highways
Repair of existing retaining walls
Common wall heights: 4-12 m; maximum approximately 18 m

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.summary: Advantages: 10–30% cost savings over conventional systems, fast top-down construction, adaptable geometry, minimal traffic disruption, and tolerance of relatively large deformations. Limitations: not suitable with large surcharges near wall crest, limited effectiveness in soft fine-grained soils or high groundwater, and corrosion concerns in aggressive environments for permanent walls.
sections.body: Advantages of soil nail walls include: lower cost than many conventional retaining wall systems (typically 10-30% savings); relatively fast construction; easily adaptable to varying site geometry and wall alignment changes; less disruptive to traffic; less right-of-way required compared to conventional cut slopes; and flexible system that can tolerate relatively large deformations without structural distress. Limitations include: not suitable where large surcharges exist close behind the wall crest; potential for excessive deformation for structures sensitive to movement; difficulty in high-groundwater conditions; limited effectiveness in soft fine-grained soils prone to creep; and corrosion concerns for permanent applications in aggressive ground conditions.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluation
sections.summary: Feasibility evaluation keys are: soil ability to stand unsupported in 1–2 m cuts for short periods, groundwater preferably below excavation bottom, wall geometry and height, deformation tolerance of nearby structures, construction access, right-of-way and utility constraints, corrosion potential, and seismic considerations.
sections.body: A feasibility evaluation should be performed early in the project to determine if soil nailing is viable. Key factors include: soil type and stratigraphy (must be able to stand in a near-vertical cut of 1-2 m for a short period); groundwater conditions (water table preferably below excavation bottom); wall geometry and height; proximity to existing structures (deformation tolerance); construction access and available equipment; right-of-way constraints and underground utilities; corrosion potential of the ground; and seismic considerations.
key_points: Evaluate soil ability to stand unsupported in 1-2 m cuts for short periods
Groundwater preferably below excavation bottom
Consider wall geometry, height, and proximity to structures
Assess deformation tolerance of nearby structures
Evaluate construction access and equipment requirements
Check right-of-way constraints and underground utilities
Assess corrosion potential and seismic considerations

sections.title: Favorable and Unfavorable Soil Conditions
sections.summary: Favorable: stiff to hard fine-grained soils with low PI, dense granular soils with apparent cohesion, weathered rock, glacial tills. Unfavorable: dry cohesionless soils (cannot stand unsupported), high groundwater, soft clays (Su < 25 kPa), organic/peat soils, highly corrosive or piping-susceptible soils. Marginal: cobbles/boulders, relict slip surfaces.
sections.body: Favorable soil conditions for soil nailing include: stiff to hard fine-grained soils with low to moderate plasticity and low moisture content; dense to very dense granular soils with apparent cohesion or cementation; weathered rock; and glacial soils (tills). Unfavorable conditions include: dry, cohesionless soils (loose sand or gravel without fines, unable to stand unsupported); soils with high groundwater; soft to very soft fine-grained soils (Su < 25 kPa); highly organic or peat soils; highly corrosive ground; soils susceptible to piping or running; expansive clays; and loess with high moisture content. Marginal conditions may include: soils with cobbles and boulders (drilling difficulties) and soils with relict slip surfaces.
key_points: Favorable: stiff to hard fine-grained soils with low PI
Favorable: dense granular soils with apparent cohesion
Favorable: weathered rock, glacial tills
Unfavorable: dry cohesionless soils that cannot stand unsupported
Unfavorable: high groundwater, soft clays (Su < 25 kPa)
Unfavorable: highly organic, highly corrosive, or piping-susceptible soils
Marginal: cobbles/boulders, relict slip surfaces

sections.title: Factors Affecting Costs
sections.summary: Primary cost driver is wall height and length. Other key factors: ground conditions and drilling method, corrosion protection level, facing type (shotcrete vs. CIP), drainage provisions, contractor experience, and project size (mobilization amortization). Compare with alternatives: soldier pile and lagging, anchored walls, MSE walls, and conventional gravity walls.
sections.body: Major factors affecting soil nail wall costs include: wall height and length (primary cost driver); soil nail length, diameter, and spacing; drilling method and ground conditions (harder ground increases cost); type and level of corrosion protection; type of facing (shotcrete vs. CIP concrete, initial vs. final facing); drainage provisions; right-of-way and access constraints; local labor and material costs; contractor experience; project size (mobilization costs amortized over larger projects); and load testing requirements. Cost comparisons should be made with alternative systems including soldier pile and lagging, anchored walls, MSE walls, and conventional gravity walls.
key_points: Primary cost driver: wall height and length
Ground conditions and drilling method significantly affect cost
Corrosion protection level affects cost substantially
Facing type: shotcrete vs CIP concrete
Compare with alternatives: soldier pile, anchored walls, MSE, gravity walls
Contractor experience and project size affect unit costs
